beats.script_body: In 2016 President Barack Obama declared Christopher Park — a small fenced-in triangle with benches and greenery in the heart of the West Village — a national park, and on it the first national monument dedicated to LGBTIQ+ history. beats.script_body: In the early 1900s the western area around the Meatpacking District and Chelsea was the largest industrial section of Manhattan. Street-level freight trains caused so much disruption and death that Tenth Ave earned the nickname 'Death Ave' for rail accidents that claimed over 500 lives. The answer was to lift the tracks: the 'West Side Elevated Line' moved its first train in 1933. The project drained over $150 million — around $2 billion in today's money — and took roughly five years to complete.

beats.script_body: On a warm spring day in 2009, the High Line opened to the public — full of blooming flowers and broad-leaved trees — the first of three phases. Section 1 starts at Gansevoort St and runs parallel to Tenth Ave up to W 20th St, filled with sitting space from giant chaises longues to bleacher-like benches. beats.source_passage: On a warm spring day in 2009, the High Line – full of blooming flowers and broad-leaved trees – opened to the public, the first of three phases that today link the Meatpacking District and Midtown. Section 1 starts at Gansevoort St and runs parallel to Tenth Ave up to W 20th St. Full of sitting space in various forms – from giant chaises longues to bleacher-like benches – the first part quickly became the setting for various public works and activities, many geared toward the neighborhood’s growing population of families. Two years later, Section 2 opened, adding another 10 blocks of greenified tracks. In 2014 the High Line’s third section was completed, from 30th up to 34th St, going up to and around the West Side Rail Yards in a U-like fashion.

beats.script_body: The iconic Stanford White Arch, known colloquially as the Washington Square Arch, dominates the park with 72ft of beaming white Dover marble. It was originally designed in wood to celebrate the centennial of George Washington's inauguration in 1889; the design proved so popular that it was replaced in stone six years later and adorned with statues of the general in war and peace. In 1916 the artist Marcel Duchamp famously climbed to the top of the arch by its internal stairway and declared the park the 'Free and Independent Republic of Washington Square.'

In 1916 artist Marcel Duchamp famously climbed to the top of the arch by its internal stairway and declared the park the ‘Free and Independent Republic of Washington Square.’

beats.script_body: Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Whitney's asymmetrical, glass-cloaked home quickly became a major landmark at the southern edge of the Meatpacking District, anchoring the first-opened section of the High Line. The nine-story cultural colossus holds galleries, theaters, classrooms and outdoor spaces — including an 18,000-sq-ft room that is New York's largest column-free exhibition space. Commenced in 2010, it cost $422 million to build and opened to great acclaim in 2015.

beats.source_passage: Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Whitney’s asymmetrical, glass-cloaked home quickly became a major landmark in the southern reaches of the Meatpacking District, housing myriad galleries, theaters, classrooms and outdoor spaces, and anchoring the first-opened section of the High Line. One gallery in particular is noteworthy – an 18,000-sq-ft space that is New York’s largest column-free exhibition space. Once the decision was made to move from the Whitney’s original, Marcel Breuer–designed home on Madison Ave, something on the scale of this nine-story cultural colossus was always likely. Commenced in 2010, it cost $422 million to build, and opened to great acclaim in 2015.

beats.script_body: The Whitney's collection of over 23,000 works by 3,000-plus American artists carries extra weight because it's all 20th- and 21st-century work, much of it by still-practising artists. Expect Sol LeWitt's Five Towers, looking like the load-bearing frame of an abandoned building; several of Andy Warhol's luridly colored Mao Tse-Tung prints; Alice Neel's portrait of Warhol, for which the pop-art legend sat while recovering from a near-fatal shooting; Jasper Johns's Three Flags; and Marsden Hartley's early-modernist Painting, Number 5.

beats.source_passage: The Whitney’s collection of over 23,000 works by 3000+ different American artists assumes greater significance when you consider it’s all 20th- and 21st-century work, much of it by still-practising artists. Works from the permanent collection you might expect to encounter include Sol LeWitt’s Five Towers (1986), looking like the load-bearing frame of an abandoned building; several of Andy Warhol’s 10 luridly colored Mao TseTung prints (1972); Alice Neel’s Andy Warhol (1970) for which the pop-art legend sat while recovering from a near-fatal shooting; Jasper Johns’s Three Flags (1958); Marsden Hartley’s early-modernist Painting, Number 5 (1914–15); and plenty of comparable treasures.
